excerpts.text: There must, however, have been interpreters of the quipus, those who, with knowledge derived from other sources, could use the knots as reminders and suggesters by which an event could be kept in memory with more accuracy. These were the Amautas, or learned men and councillors. For them the quipus formed a system of reminders, giving accuracy to knowledge derived from other methods of recording events and traditions. For it cannot be supposed that the system of different coloured knots could do more than supply a sort of aid to memory, or a memoria technica. It is, however, certain that the traditions and records of events were preserved by the Amautas with considerable exactness. There is, for instance, the Paccari-tampu myth. It is told by Garcilasso de la Vega, Cieza de Leon, Betanzos, Balboa, Morua, Montesinos, Salcamayhua and Sarmiento, all agreeing sufficiently closely to prove that precisely the same tradition had been handed down, with the same details, to their various informants. Similarly the details of the Chanca war and other principal events were preserved.
excerpts.speaker: Clements Robert Markham

excerpts.text: 'The Amautas composed both tragedies and comedies, which were represented before the Inca and his court on solemn occasions. The subject matter of the tragedy related to military deeds and the victories of former times; while the arguments of the comedies were on agricultural and familiar household subjects. They understood the composition of long and short verses, with the right number of syllables in each. They did not use rhymes in the verses.'

excerpts.text: This Convention is not four days old, and the melodious Melibœan stanzas that shook down Royalty are still fresh in our ear, when there bursts out a new diapason,—unhappily, of Discord, this time. For speech has been made of a thing difficult to speak of well: the September Massacres. How deal with these September Massacres; with the Paris Commune that presided over them? A Paris Commune hateful-terrible; before which the poor effete Legislative had to quail, and sit quiet. And now if a young omnipotent Convention will not so quail and sit, what steps shall it take? Have a Departmental Guard in its pay, answer the Girondins and Friends of Order! A Guard of National Volunteers, missioned from all the Eighty-three or Eighty-five Departments, for that express end; these will keep Septemberers, tumultuous Communes in a due state of submissiveness, the Convention in a due state of sovereignty. So have the Friends of Order answered, sitting in Committee, and reporting; and even a Decree has been passed of the required tenour. Nay certain Departments, as the Var or Marseilles, in mere expectation and assurance of a Decree, have their contingent of Volunteers already on march; brave Marseillese, foremost on the Tenth of August, will not be hindmost here: 'fathers gave their sons a musket and twenty-five louis,' says Barbaroux, 'and bade them march.'

excerpts.text: A Republic that will found itself on justice must needs investigate September Massacres; a Convention calling itself National, ought it not to be guarded by a National force?—Alas, Reader, it seems so to the eye: and yet there is much to be said and argued. Thou beholdest here the small beginning of a Controversy, which mere logic will not settle. Two small well-springs, September, Departmental Guard, or rather at bottom they are but one and the same small well-spring; which will swell and widen into waters of bitterness; all manner of subsidiary streams and brooks of bitterness flowing in, from this side and that; till it become a wide river of bitterness, of rage and separation,—which can subside only into the Catacombs. This Departmental Guard, decreed by overwhelming majorities, and then repealed for peace's sake, and not to insult Paris, is again decreed more than once; nay it is partially executed, and the very men that are to be of it

excerpts.text: But on this fourth day of the Convention's existence, as we said, which is the 25th of September 1792, there comes Committee Report on that Decree of the Departmental Guard, and speech of repealing it; there come denunciations of Anarchy, of a Dictatorship,—which let the incorruptible Robespierre consider: there come denunciations of a certain Journal de la République , once called Ami du Peuple ; and so thereupon there comes, visibly stepping up, visibly standing aloft on the Tribune, ready to speak,—the Bodily Spectrum of People's-Friend Marat! Shriek, ye Seven-hundred and Forty-nine; it is verily Marat, he and not another. Marat is no phantasm of the brain, or mere lying impress of Printer's Types; but a thing material, of joint and sinew, and a certain small stature; ye behold him there, in his blackness, in his dingy squalor, a living fraction of Chaos and Old Night; visibly incarnate, desirous to speak. 'It appears,' says Marat to the shrieking Assembly, 'that a great many persons here are enemies of mine.'—'All! all!' shriek hundreds of voices: enough to drown any People's-Friend. But Marat will not drown: he speaks and croaks explanation; croaks with such reasonableness, air of sincerity, that repentant pity smothers anger, and the shrieks subside, or even become applauses.
excerpts.speaker: Thomas Carlyle
excerpts.episodeTitle: The September Massacres
excerpts.documentTitle: The Works of Thomas Carlyle/Volume 4/The French Revolution, Volume 3/Book 2

excerpts.text: Thus Marat, absolved and applauded, victorious in this turn of fence, is, as the Debate goes on, prickt at again by some dexterous Girondin; and then the shrieks rise anew, and Decree of Accusation is on the point of passing; till the dingy People's-Friend bobs aloft once more; croaks once more persuasive stillness, and the Decree of Accusation sinks.

excerpts.text: Behind the entrenched armies was an intricate mesh of railways, not to mention the roads on which petrol-driven vehicles would soon be crowding; the British Army, which in August 1914 had only 100 motor lorries, possessed 60,000 of them at the end of the war. More than anything else, it was these modern facilities of transport that differentiated the 'great' war of 1914-18 from wars of the pre-railway age, great though they, too, may have been when measured against the technical capacities of their own time. Twentieth-century transport could carry food, fuel and clothing sufficient to maintain in continuous array of battle, armies that were now reckoned by the million, and it could carry as much ammunition as the factories could produce to feed their modernised weapons. More men, more numerous, powerful and intricate equipment, a vastly increased rate of consumption and wastage—here was the immediate pull of demand which transformed the economic effort of war. Faced with this unprecedented demand, supply faltered and failed. From the failure of supply emerged something new:

excerpts.text: Sonderkommando Salmen Gradowski kept a diary of his experiences at the camp which he buried in an aluminium can. Schlomo Dragon remembered where it was buried. Remarkably the can and its contents were found intact and dug up after the liberation of the camp. The can contained a notebook and a letter dated 6th September 1944. In the letter Gradowski explained that it was his aim to preserve a written account of what had happened at Auschwitz. He wrote that this task became even more important once the Nazis started to burn the bodies of those they had killed and to dispose of the ashes in the River Vistula. He said that he and fellow Sonderkommandos had scattered the teeth of the dead over a wide area so that they might be found by subsequent generations. Gradowski claimed that the Jewish nation had been destroyed in the camps. He recorded that he and fellow camp workers had planned a mutiny. (The uprising took place in October 1944.

excerpts.text: In 1807, Lord Granville brought into the House of Lords, "A bill for the Abolition of the Slave Trade." Counsel was heard against the bill for four days. The subject was then thoroughly discussed—and the bill passed with a majority of 100 to 36. In the Commons the majority in its favor was 283 against 16. It passed the Commons on 10th February, 1807.

excerpts.text: A committee of the whole House being then formed, a bill was immediately passed, "that no vessel should clear out for slaves, from any port within the British dominions, after 1st May, 1807;" and "that no slave should be landed in the Colonies after 1st March, 1808." This bill was passed on 16th March, 1807, and through the strenuous exertions of Lord Granville, received the royal assent on Wednesday, 25th, a few minutes only before the ministers resigned their respective offices, as they had been required to do, by a message delivered to them that morning.

premise: A source-conscious historical survey of human aggressiveness across eras and regions, examining how ecology, technology, institutions, inequality, ideology, social identity, and political power have shaped violence without reducing history to a single theory of human nature.
audience: General readers curious about history who want a clear, balanced account of why aggressive behavior and organized violence have varied across societies and periods.

chapters.title: What Do We Mean by Human Aggression?
chapters.summary: Establish working distinctions among anger, interpersonal violence, raiding, warfare, coercive law, and organized atrocity. Introduce the problem of uneven historical evidence and explain why the book compares cases without assuming a universal scale of aggression.
keyBeats: Open with a documented setting where several forms of coercion coexist.
Define the book's terms in accessible language.
Explain how historians, archaeologists, and other researchers infer past behavior.
Set expectations for regional comparison and evidentiary uncertainty.

chapters.title: Before States: Small Communities and the Archaeological Record
chapters.summary: Examine what burials, injuries, settlement patterns, tools, and ecological evidence can and cannot reveal about violence before written states. Avoid treating isolated remains as direct measures of everyday aggression.
keyBeats: Begin with a specific archaeological site or burial context whose interpretation is debated.
Distinguish individual injury from organized conflict.
Consider mobility, resources, kinship, and population density as possible influences.
End by showing why absence of evidence is also difficult to interpret.

chapters.title: Cities, Kings, and the Invention of Organized War
chapters.summary: Explore early urban societies and the relationship among surplus, hierarchy, fortification, labor, taxation, and military power. Use cases from more than one region to test whether state formation consistently increased or redirected violence.
keyBeats: Introduce an early city, ruler, inscription, or defensive structure.
Separate royal propaganda from independent evidence where possible.
Trace how administration made coercion more durable.
Compare at least two early state contexts without forcing equivalence.

chapters.title: Empires and the Management of Difference
chapters.summary: Study imperial expansion, tribute, deportation, frontier warfare, and negotiated rule through selected ancient and classical empires. Focus on how violence and accommodation operated together.
keyBeats: Open with a frontier, road, census, monument, or captured population.
Show how imperial records justify force.
Examine local intermediaries and forms of resistance.
Assess when coercion stabilized rule and when it produced revolt.

chapters.title: Warriors, Cities, and Moral Order in the Americas
chapters.summary: Survey selected societies in North, Central, and South America before and during early colonial contact, with care around varied evidence and later interpretation. Consider ritual, political authority, captive-taking, alliance, and environmental pressures.
keyBeats: Begin with a specific city, polity, community, or material record.
Distinguish ceremonial representations from evidence of practice.
Explain how alliance and diplomacy shaped conflict.
Address the distortions introduced by conquest-era observers.

chapters.title: Frontiers, Faiths, and Political Fragmentation
chapters.summary: Examine medieval and post-classical worlds across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Middle East, where raiding, dynastic conflict, religious authority, trade, and frontier politics intersected.
keyBeats: Open in a documented frontier or contested city.
Compare mobile raiding with settled state warfare.
Show how religious language could authorize, constrain, or reinterpret violence.
Include ordinary people, not only rulers and commanders.

chapters.title: Steppe Powers and Connected Worlds
chapters.summary: Investigate steppe confederations, mounted warfare, trade routes, migration, and conquest across Eurasia. Avoid reducing mobile societies to violence by examining administration, exchange, diplomacy, and cultural mixture.
keyBeats: Introduce a route, camp, city, or surviving administrative record.
Explain the tactical and ecological conditions of mobility.
Trace how conquest altered populations and institutions.
Balance destruction narratives with evidence of integration and governance.

chapters.title: States, Slavery, and the Atlantic World
chapters.summary: Analyze early modern expansion, plantation economies, enslavement, maritime power, Indigenous resistance, and state violence around the Atlantic. Keep economic incentives connected to law, ideology, and local agency.
keyBeats: Open with a documented port, plantation, ship, court record, or community.
Explain how law converted violence into an institution.
Follow both perpetrators' rationalizations and the actions of enslaved people.
Distinguish regional systems rather than treating the Atlantic as uniform.

chapters.title: Gunpowder, Bureaucracy, and Mass Mobilization
chapters.summary: Explore how firearms, fiscal systems, standing armies, taxation, and bureaucratic states changed the scale and organization of violence in selected regions from the early modern period.
keyBeats: Begin with a battle plan, arsenal, tax register, or military reform.
Trace the link between state capacity and military reach.
Show how civilians experienced requisition, displacement, and law.
Test whether technology changed motives or mainly changed capacity.

chapters.title: Revolution and the Politics of the Crowd
chapters.summary: Examine revolutions, popular violence, civil conflict, and political ideology from the eighteenth through nineteenth centuries. Consider rumor, legitimacy, class, race, citizenship, and institutional collapse.
keyBeats: Open with a documented crowd action or public trial.
Distinguish spontaneous violence from organized political campaigns.
Show how revolutionary language made violence meaningful to participants.
Explain why restraint sometimes survived amid institutional crisis.

chapters.title: Colonial Rule and Resistance
chapters.summary: Study colonial conquest, forced labor, policing, boundaries, extraction, and anti-colonial resistance across Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and other regions. Make room for collaboration, adaptation, and competing local interests.
keyBeats: Begin with a specific encounter, ordinance, map, labor site, or uprising.
Identify the institutions that made coercion routine.
Avoid presenting colonized societies as passive recipients of violence.
Compare colonial systems while preserving their distinct histories.

chapters.title: Industrial War and the Civilian Population
chapters.summary: Explain how railways, factories, communications, conscription, nationalism, and modern administration expanded the reach of war from the nineteenth into the twentieth century.
keyBeats: Open with a documented civilian experience tied to industrial logistics.
Connect technology to organization rather than technological destiny.
Trace the changing boundary between battlefield and home front.
Use measured language for mass suffering and disputed estimates.

chapters.title: Genocide, Total War, and Ideological Violence
chapters.summary: Examine selected twentieth-century cases of exterminatory policy, total war, forced displacement, and political terror. Focus on warning signs, institutions, choices, and evidence rather than spectacle or a single universal model.
keyBeats: Start with a document, order, registry, site, or survivor testimony whose provenance is clear.
Show how ordinary institutions participated in extraordinary violence.
Distinguish intent, policy, implementation, and consequence.
State where historians disagree and why.

chapters.title: After 1945: Deterrence, Insurgency, and Uneven Decline
chapters.summary: Survey postwar interstate conflict, civil wars, decolonization, insurgency, proxy warfare, and changing international norms. Assess claims about declining violence cautiously and distinguish battlefield deaths from other forms of harm.
keyBeats: Open with a specific postwar conflict or negotiation.
Explain how nuclear weapons altered interstate calculations without ending war.
Examine the political conditions behind insurgency and counterinsurgency.
Separate broad trends from regional exceptions and measurement problems.

chapters.title: What History Can and Cannot Explain
chapters.summary: Synthesize the survey without claiming a final theory of human nature. Revisit the roles of ecology, institutions, inequality, technology, identity, leadership, and contingency, then close with a disciplined account of what historical comparison makes visible.
keyBeats: Return to the opening distinction between aggression and organized violence.
Bring together several cases that genuinely illuminate one another.
Identify explanations that remain contested or underdetermined.
Close with a bounded conclusion about human choices and historical conditions.

rules: Identify the type and limits of evidence before drawing conclusions.
Do not treat surviving records as representative of every social group.
Keep chronology, geography, and provenance explicit.
Separate documented fact from interpretation and uncertainty.
locations.description: The changing body of archaeological remains, inscriptions, chronicles, legal records, administrative documents, oral histories, material evidence, testimony, and later scholarship used to study aggression across eras and regions.

voiceGuide: Write in clear, accessible historical prose for general readers.
Anchor each major claim in identifiable evidence, while distinguishing documented evidence from interpretation.
Compare regions carefully without treating Europe, states, or warfare as the default measure of human aggression.
Use concrete people, places, objects, practices, and historical moments before drawing bounded conclusions.
Explain competing interpretations fairly, then state what the available evidence supports most securely.
Keep the tone neutral, humane, and moderately confident; acknowledge uncertainty when the record is incomplete.
Treat aggression as a set of behaviors and institutions rather than a timeless substance inside humanity.
Vary chapter openings, paragraph lengths, transitions, and endings.
Connect local histories to wider patterns only after supplying chronology and context.
antiAiRules: Do not invent studies, statistics, experts, institutions, citations, archaeological findings, or source identities.
Do not imply that one cause explains aggression across all societies or eras.
Do not treat incomplete records as transparent evidence of ordinary behavior.
Avoid proof-leap phrases such as "the truth is," "hidden in plain sight," and "no accident" unless directly quoted or necessary.
Avoid repeated binary reversals such as "X is not A. It is B."
Do not stack adjacent contrast sentences that leap from a fact to a sweeping conclusion.
Use em dashes and en dashes sparingly.
Replace inflated abstractions with concrete examples and precise qualifications.
Do not generalize from rulers, armies, laws, or surviving texts to entire populations without qualification.
Do not mention prompts, AI, planning, generation, schemas, or production instructions in reader-facing prose.
Do not end every chapter with the same summary formula or question.
Do not force the same causal framework onto every region.
Do not turn historical suffering into spectacle or use graphic detail for atmosphere.
Do not present moral condemnation as historical explanation.
Present the concrete evidence and its limits before offering an interpretation.
Define the relevant form of aggression in context, distinguishing interpersonal violence, raiding, warfare, coercion, and state punishment.
Keep dates, sequences, political entities, and regional boundaries explicit enough for a general reader to follow.
Name the particular society, locality, institution, or group under discussion instead of using vague regional labels.
Treat causal explanations as combinations of conditions unless evidence strongly supports a narrower claim.
Avoid unsupported proof-leap transitions; do not jump from a local fact to a sweeping conclusion without evidence on this page.
Do not invent evidence, citations, studies, experts, or source identities.

openingHook: At a prehistoric burial site, a healed fracture and a lethal wound can sit in the same soil, inviting two different questions: what happened to these people, and what can anyone responsibly infer from the traces they left behind?

authorStance.thesis: Human aggressiveness has appeared in many societies, but its scale, targets, and meaning have been shaped decisively by institutions, resources, technologies, identities, and historical choices.
refusals: I refuse to turn isolated examples into universal laws about humanity.
I refuse to present perpetrators' explanations as complete accounts of their actions.
I refuse to balance every interpretation mechanically when the evidence supports a bounded conclusion.
I refuse to use suffering as spectacle or certainty as a substitute for sources.
positions: Violence in history is organised before it is felt: someone decides who may be harmed, and that decision leaves a record.
The offices that police a state's own subjects are the offices that build harm on a scale no feud reaches.
Scarcity becomes killing where an authority has already decided who may be dispossessed.
Every weapon in this book was pointed by an institution, and the institution is the subject.
The differences between two societies' violence are the finding, and they carry the argument.
authorStance.voiceSample: In 1919, a railway timetable in central Europe carried more than departure times between stations. Its columns linked towns, factories, military depots, and food markets inside a political landscape still unsettled by the First World War. A clerk reading the page could see movement as routine administration; a family waiting beside a platform could experience the same system as separation, delay, or escape. At the Hôtel Lutetia in Paris, diplomats handled maps whose colored borders compressed villages, languages, and memories into negotiable shapes. The pencil marks looked provisional, yet the decisions attached to them could redirect schools, taxes, and police authority for decades. In a notebook from a dockworker in Marseille, the price of coal appeared beside the names of ships and absent men. Such objects resist a clean division between economics and politics. The timetable, map, and notebook belong to different settings, but each records a choice about movement and control. Their value lies in their limits as much as their detail. None can speak for every traveler, diplomat, or worker. Together, they make a narrower point: large historical changes often enter ordinary lives through paperwork, waiting rooms, wages, and borders.
